# Readings

My father kept a record of the weather every day for forty-one years.

I found the notebooks after the funeral, in the bottom drawer of the desk in the garage, the drawer I had always assumed held tax returns. There were sixty-three of them, the cheap kind with marbled covers, each one labeled on the spine in black marker with a start date and an end date. The earliest began in March of the year I was born.

Every entry followed the same format. Date. High and low temperature, taken from the thermometer nailed to the fence post by the tomato beds. Precipitation, measured in a plastic rain gauge I remembered knocking over with a soccer ball when I was nine. Wind, described rather than measured: *calm*, *light from W*, *gusty*, *strong, took the lid off the bin*. Sky. And then, at the end of each line, a single short remark.

The remarks were what undid me.

Most of them were about the weather itself. *Fog burned off by ten.* *First frost, lost the basil.* *Hail, small, didn't last.* But scattered among them, sometimes weeks apart, sometimes months, were other things.

*K. walked today. Four steps to the couch.*

K. is me.

*K. home from school sick. Watched cartoons together. Rain all afternoon, which suited us.*

*M.'s mother passed. Clear and cold. M. sat outside a long time.*

M. was my mother.

I sat on the concrete floor of the garage with the notebooks spread around me in a half circle and read for four hours. I read the year my parents almost separated, which I had not known about, and which I understood only from a stretch of entries in which the remarks disappeared entirely for eleven weeks, just numbers, and then returned with: *M. and I talked. Mild. Wind dropped in the evening.* I read the day I left for college: *Overcast. K. gone. House very quiet. 71/54.* I read the week my mother was diagnosed, and the long gray months after, the remarks getting shorter and shorter until they were single words. *Hospital.* *Hospital.* *Home.* *Better.* *Worse.*

The day she died, he wrote the temperatures, the rainfall, the wind, the sky, and then nothing. The next day, the same. He didn't write another remark for almost two years. But he never missed a reading. Not one day. I checked.

I don't know what to make of a man who could not skip measuring the rain the morning after his wife died. For a while I thought it was coldness, or a kind of avoidance, the engineer's retreat into numbers when feelings got too big. That's how I'd always thought of him: reliable, reserved, a man who expressed love by checking the tire pressure on your car before a long drive.

But I don't think that anymore.

I think the readings were how he stayed. I think going out to the fence post every morning, in his robe, in the dark, in the snow, was a promise he kept to the world that he would keep paying attention to it, even when paying attention was the hardest thing he could do. I think the weather was the one thing that kept arriving no matter what, and he wanted to be there to meet it.

The last entry was eight days before he died. His handwriting had gotten shaky by then, the numbers leaning into each other. *Sunny, warm for October. 68/49. Leaves turning on the maple. K. called.*

I did call. I remember it. We talked for maybe ten minutes, mostly about whether he'd been taking his pills, and I was distracted, making dinner, and I said I'd call again on the weekend. I didn't. Something came up. I don't even remember what.

*K. called.* That's all. No complaint that it was short. No note that I'd promised to call back. Just the fact of it, set down beside the leaves and the temperature, as though my voice on the phone were one more condition of the day worth recording. As though it counted.

---

I brought the thermometer home. I had to pry it off the fence post with a screwdriver, and the post was so old that a strip of gray wood came away with it. The rain gauge was cracked, so I bought a new one, glass this time. I mounted them both on the railing of my apartment balcony, which faces east, over a parking lot and a row of sycamores and, beyond that, the freeway.

I bought a notebook with a marbled cover.

It has been four months now. I take the readings in the morning before work, with my coffee going cold on the railing beside me. I am not as disciplined as he was. I've missed eleven days. On those days I leave the line blank rather than guess, because guessing seems like a kind of lie, and I think he would have agreed.

Mostly I just write the numbers. But some days I add something at the end.

*Rain overnight, 0.4 in. Sycamores dripping.*

*Cold. Saw my breath for the first time this year.*

*Called Aunt Ruth. She told me the story about Dad and the goat again. Still funny.*

*Clear. 52/38. Missed him.*

I don't know who I'm writing them for. There is no one to find these notebooks in a drawer someday. Maybe that's fine. Maybe the point was never to be found.

This morning it was foggy, the kind of fog that erases the freeway and makes the parking lot feel like the edge of the ocean. I stood on the balcony and couldn't see the sycamores at all, only hear them, the soft tick of water falling from leaf to leaf. It was quiet in a way the city almost never is.

I wrote it down. The temperature, the sky, the wind, which was calm. And then, after a while, because it was true:

*Paying attention.*
